newsitem.title: Zaire: Zairean rebels demand power, say will fight on.
newsitem.headline: Zairean rebels demand power, say will fight on.

text.p: Zairean rebel leader Laurent Kabila said on Sunday his forces would fight on while President Mobutu Sese Seko considered their demand he resign.

Kabila, head of the Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo-Zaire (ADFL), told Reuters in an interview by satellite phone from a South African navy ship that his frontline units were closing in on Kinshasa airport.
"Mobutu has asked me to give him eight days while he considers our demand to resign," said Kabila.

"I have agreed to that request and we shall meet again on this same ship within the next eight days. But I have told him and the mediators that there will be no ceasefire while he considers our demands.

"I made it clear a ceasefire is out of the question and my forces will continue to advance on all fronts. If we make it to Kinshasa before the eight days then too bad but we cannot wait while he makes up his mind," he added.

U.N. and Organisation of African Unity (OAU) special envoy Mohamed Sahnoun, reading a final communique after the talks, told a closing news conference on board the SAS Outeniqu that Mobutu had offered to hand over to an elected president.
Kabila, for his part, insisted that his rebel alliance should act as the transitional authority to organise elections, the communique said.
South African President Nelson Mandela told the news conference Kabila ordered his forces to stop advancing ahead of the talks but that this did not constitute a ceasefire.
"The question of a ceasefire is not part of his (Kabila's) vocabulary. What he is concerned with is that negotiations will lead to the end of hostilities," he added.
Kabila's rebels have captured more than three quarters of the vast country in seven months and Mobutu's forces have hardly put up any resistance to their rapid advance.

A mining manager on Sunday quoted his Kinshasa office as saying the rebels were within 40 miles (65 km) of Kinshasa airport and had taken the large town of Mbanza-Ngungu, which lies southwest of the capital.
At Lubumbashi international airport, hundreds of rebel soldiers boarded planes taking them to the front lines. Heavy equipment was also being loaded on cargo planes.
Kabila's "foreign minister", Bizima Karaha, told Reuters earlier that the rebels rejected Mobutu's proposal that he hand power to some third party.
"Mobutu wants power transferred to another person, who in turn would negotiate with president Kabila, but for us that's unacceptable. Power must go directly to our president," he said.
"Mobutu has agreed to resign but he wants authority transferred to an interim body and this is what we are negotiating about now," he added.
Back in Lubumbashi, a senior commander told Reuters that rebel forces were closing in on the town of Bandundu, 260 km (160 miles) northeast of Kinshasa.
"Our forces are near Bandundu. They are near enough to take out Mobutu's troops. The town should go any time," he said.
He said rebels were also about to enter Businga and Gemena, towns which lie between the rebels and Mobutu's jungle palace at Gbadolite near the border with the Central African Republic.
"Reports from the field commanders are that both Businga and Gemena are now vulnerable and should be entered any time from now. We have detected no resistance," he added.
Residents of the Kenge area, 200 km (120 miles) southeast of the capital, said Kabila's rebels were massing nearby.
One resident said that large numbers of rebel troops had been leaving Masi-Manimba, 300 km (190 miles) from Kinshasa along the same road, to assemble at Kenge.
